U3 LANDOWNERS’ REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

           U3 Landowners1 hereby timely file this Reply to Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision
(PFD) and, in support thereof, would show the following.


                   I.      SUMMARY OF REPLY TO ROUTING EXCEPTIONS
          The routing portions of the PFD should be adopted as written. The PFD recognizes that
every Focus Route has advantages and disadvantages, weighs those tradeoffs under the
Commission’s routing criteria, and finds that Route 894 presents an appropriate balance. Brady
Creek, Solana, Staten Creek, and 4K Land and Cattle ask the ALJs and Commission to assign
controlling weight to selected factors or to a party’s scoring model. Their exceptions do not
establish that the PFD overlooked material routing evidence or misapplied a routing criterion. The
ALJs should decline to modify any routing portion of the PFD, and the Commission should


1
    U3 Landowners: 3 Trees Ranch Family, LP, Edward Cambon, Karen Cambon, Julie & Larry Williams, John &
    Karen Sloan, Pepper Isom, George and Barbara Ellington, Leah Snell, Jan Klose, Dustin Duncan, Keith & Kathy
    Duncan, Duncan FLP, 4E Edgar Ranch LP, Rick Carroll, Michael & Linda Joseph, Les Hardy, School Creek Ranch,

    Shahan, James & Kimberly Burkett, Jake Burnett.
 overrule the routing exceptions and adopt the PFD’s routing analysis, proposed routing findings,
and recommendation of Route 894 without change.2


    II.      THE ALJs DID NOT ERR IN THEIR COMPARATIVE EVALUATION OF
                                 ROUTES 894 AND 392
          The PFD evaluated complete routes rather than allowing one link or one subset of the
routing data to control. The record evidence shows Route 894 performs favorably on cost, length,
habitable structures, compatible right-of-way, rangeland pasture, and riparian areas. The PFD’s
data show that Route 894 parallels or uses 98.0 miles of compatible right-of-way, or 43.9 percent
of its length, compared with 88.5 miles and 38.6 percent for Route 392. Thus, even if Route 392
has more transmission-line paralleling, Route 894 outperforms 392 on total compatible right-of-
way.3     The PFD also found that Route 392 has notably more habitable structures and cultural
resources. The exceptions identify no error in that complete-route comparison. The ALJs should
decline to alter it, and the Commission should adopt it as written.4
          Brady Creek and Solana’s exceptions ask the Commission to dismiss the habitable-
structure disparity by downplaying the importance of prudent avoidance. Put directly, Route 392
would place the line within 500 feet of 51 additional habitable structures—136 instead of 85, a
60 percent increase—and would cost approximately $34 million more. The PFD did not find
Route 392 prohibited—it found that Route 894 achieves prudent avoidance more effectively. That
comparative judgment follows the policy’s purpose of limiting avoidable exposure. The ALJs and
Commission should reject the invitation to erase that distinction5 and should leave the PFD’s
finding6 unchanged.
          In Dunn v. Public Utility Commission of Texas, the Austin Court of Appeals rejected an
argument materially similar to the one advanced by Brady Creek and Solana.7 The landowners in
Dunn argued that the Commission’s failure to select one of two routes that paralleled more existing
rights-of-way and property lines than the selected route was arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of
discretion, and not supported by substantial evidence. The court rejected the premise that a


2
  See PFD at 102, 142–48; proposed Findings of Fact 152–76. All page references are to printed page numbers.
3
  PFD at 139.
4
  PFD at 102, 139, 142–48.
5
  Brady Creek Exceptions at 29–30; Solana Exceptions at 24–26.
6
  PFD at 102, 143–47; proposed Findings of Fact 167–68.
7
  Dunn v. Pub. Util. Comm’n of Tex., 246 S.W.3d 788, 795–96 & n.5 (Tex. App.—Austin 2008, no pet.)
 numerical advantage on a single criterion compels route selection regardless of the remaining
evidence, holding that the rule does not permit “exclusive reliance on the numerical percentage”
of rights-of-way used or paralleled and that “no one factor controls or is dispositive.”8 Brady
Creek and Solana ask the Commission to go further still: they elevate one application of one
routing criterion at a single stream crossing over the complete route comparison, even though
Route 392 costs $34.299 million more, affects 51 more habitable structures, and performs worse
on multiple environmental and cultural-resource measures.
           PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) require holistic route-selection
judgment. The Commission must consider community values, parks and recreational areas,
historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, engineering constraints, cost, prudent
avoidance, and the use of compatible corridors.              Dunn establishes that no single factor is
dispositive. The governing framework therefore does not permit Route 392’s proponents to
transform paralleling at U3 into a bright-line rule that automatically defeats every route crossing
the Colorado River elsewhere.


    III.     THE ALJs DID NOT ERR IN WEIGHING PARK AND TERRAIN IMPACTS
           Brady Creek, Staten Creek, and 4K emphasize Route 894’s visibility from and proximity
to two parks.9 The PFD expressly acknowledged Route 894 would be visible from areas of both
parks and nonetheless recommended 894 after weighing the competing route-specific factors. The
exceptions identify no park evidence the PFD failed to consider. They ask the ALJs and
Commission to reverse the routing recommendation by making this factor dispositive, despite
Route 894’s advantages in habitable structures, total compatible right-of-way, and cultural
resources. The ALJs should reject that attempted reweighing, and the Commission should leave
the PFD’s treatment10 of this factor unchanged.
           4K, relying on testimony from its witness Luther King, also argues that Route 894 crosses
more difficult terrain. But the U3 Landowners’ testimony identified specific construction and
environmental concerns along Link U3, including steep access, existing erosion, multiple tributary




8
  Id.
9
  Brady Creek Exceptions at 19–24; Staten Creek Exceptions at 3–21, 28; 4K Exceptions at 13–20.
10
   PFD at 117, 147–48.
 crossings, and sensitive river habitat. 4K’s evidence does nothing to refute the documented
impacts at Link U3. The ALJs and Commission should decline to revise the PFD on that basis.11


     IV.     THE 4K MODEL DOES NOT ESTABLISH ERROR IN THE PFD ROUTING
                                     ANALYSIS
           4K argues that the PFD should be changed because its expert’s model ranked Route 894
eighty-third and placed Northern Corridor routes at the top.12 The PFD discussed that model and
the conflicting testimony about weighted scoring.13 A party’s scoring model reflects its author’s
selected weights; it does not replace the ALJs’ duty to weigh the Commission’s routing criteria.
Agreement among scenarios generated within the model shows internal consistency, not error in
the PFD’s independent balancing. The model also does not decide the weight due Route 894’s
residential and cultural-resource advantages or the U3 Landowners’ site-specific evidence.14 The
ALJs and Commission should decline to substitute 4K’s model for the PFD’s routing analysis.


       V.       THE ALJs DID NOT ERR BY DECLINING TO TREAT LINK U3 AS A
                                 ROUTING REQUIREMENT
           Brady Creek, Solana, and Staten Creek argue that the Colorado River crossing on Link U3
should effectively control route selection because it parallels an existing 138-kV transmission
line.15     The PFD considered that point.           Although Route 392 has more transmission-line
paralleling, Route 894 outperforms 392 on total compatible right-of-way—43.9 percent to 38.6
percent. The exceptions would elevate a single stream crossing and one subset of the right-of-way
data over the PFD’s complete-route analysis. The ALJs should decline to do so, and the
Commission should retain the PFD’s balancing.16
           The exceptions17 also understate the incremental impacts of using Link U3. The U3
Landowners’ testimony compared the proposed 200-foot corridor and structures up to
approximately 198 feet tall with the existing 75-foot easement and approximately 80-foot poles.18

   4K Exceptions at 15–16; U3 Landowners Ex. 1 at 17–24.
12
   4K Exceptions at 7–10, 26–27.
13
   PFD at 107–08, 143–48.

   U3 Landowners Ex. 1 at 17–24.
15

16
   See PFD at 139, 142–48.
17
   Solana Exceptions at 27–29.
18
   U3 Landowners Ex. 1 at 17–24.
 It also identified steep access, existing erosion, multiple tributary crossings, an Ecologically
Significant Stream Segment, and Texas pimpleback critical habitat at Link U3. Link U3 crosses
and then parallels the Colorado River for approximately two miles, while Route 894’s crossing
leaves the river more directly. The existing line does not make Link U3 an already-cleared
corridor. The ALJs and Commission should decline to treat Link U3 as a threshold routing
requirement.
        Solana exceptions do not merely overread Staff witness Poole’s testimony; they misstate it
as an independent recommendation for a northern Colorado River crossing.19 Staff witness Poole
did not recommend Route 392 or any route using Link U3. Staff’s filed recommendation was
Route 487, while Applicants recommended Route 894, and neither route uses Link U3. Staff
doubled down on Route 487 in its exceptions.20 Testimony that one characteristic may favor a
link is not a route recommendation.              The ALJs and Commission should reject Solana’s
characterization and leave the PFD unchanged.21


                                          VI.     CONCLUSION
        The routing exceptions repeat arguments the ALJs heard and ask the decision-makers to
assign different weight to selected evidence. They do not identify a basis to disturb the PFD’s
routing judgment. U3 Landowners respectfully request that the ALJs and Commission decline to
modify any routing portion of the PFD and adopt all portions of the PFD addressing route selection;
including the proposed routing findings and recommendation of Route 894, as written; and grant
U3 Landowners all other relief to which they may be entitled.
